question: Can exhaustive tuning on language models as small as 4M effective parameters recover trustworthy parameter-data scaling laws and a known architecture choice at larger held-out scales, and what change in the hyperparameter loss surface explains transfer from small to larger models?

key_findings.claim: At small scale, hyperparameter search depth is the decisive condition for seeing a scaling law; common methodological refinements improve an already visible law but do not substitute for reaching the tuned frontier.
key_findings.evidence: With 4 or 16 sampled configurations per scale the law is absent or incomplete, with 64 it is visible but extrapolates weakly, and with 256 it becomes accurate. Separately, tuning at each parameter-token budget halves test MSE and adding learning-rate decay cuts it by 98%, while parameter-count conventions change the fit comparatively little and tying the two scaling exponents has inconsistent validation/test effects.

key_findings.claim: Random hyperparameter draws become more likely to be near-optimal as model parameters and training data grow together, and the fitted intrinsic dimension of the near-optimal loss surface falls toward one.
key_findings.evidence: Random-search loss distributions concentrate near their minima with scale, while percentile-to-minimum gaps shrink primarily when both parameters and data are large. Fits of the noisy-quadratic tail estimate the effective hyperparameter count gamma decreasing with model size toward one; the parameter axis drives most of this decline and the token-budget axis much less.

key_findings.claim: A small-scale scaling law can be locally predictive without supporting arbitrarily long quantitative extrapolation.
key_findings.evidence: Independent laws fit from 128 runs at each of 4M, 8M, 17M, and 34M parameters agree near the observations but diverge far away because the extrapolation becomes dominated by separately estimated irreducible-loss terms. The appendix likewise finds that scale-aware models of the full hyperparameter surface remain orders of magnitude less accurate than predicting only the tuned frontier.

key_findings.claim: The proposed diagnostic workflow recovers the established preference for Pre-Norm over Post-Norm from small-model experiments, but the conclusion depends partly on qualitative evidence and a shared-asymptote assumption.
key_findings.evidence: The case study samples 511/512/128 Post-Norm configurations at 4M/34M/134M effective parameters and 128 Pre-Norm configurations at each scale. Both reach a noisy-quadratic tail, but Post-Norm has a smaller tail and a persistent suboptimal mode; Pre-Norm extrapolates better and scales better over the measured range. Beyond that range, Pre-Norm remains favored only when both architectures are constrained to share the same irreducible loss; allowing separate asymptotes predicts an eventual reversal that the data do not adjudicate.

key_findings.claim: The resulting methodology is explicitly restricted to model-centric comparisons on fixed pretraining data.
key_findings.evidence: The workflow combines a noisy-quadratic tail diagnostic, a tuned-frontier scaling law, and the empirical correspondence between pretraining loss and downstream capability. The authors state that changing data breaks that correspondence, so neither pretraining loss nor currently unreliable downstream scaling laws justify carrying data-centric conclusions upward.

method.core_idea: Treat small-scale model research as a controlled search over a near-optimal hyperparameter surface, verify that the search has entered its noisy-quadratic tail, fit a parameter-data law only to the tuned frontier, and use fixed-data loss-capability correspondence plus held-out larger scales to decide whether an architectural result transfers.
method.mechanism: The authors train Llama-style decoder models on a fixed FineWeb-Edu subset at effective sizes from roughly 4M to 268M. A warmup-stable-decay schedule yields stable and decayed checkpoints at eight token budgets per run. Large random searches vary optimizer and architectural hyperparameters; noisy-quadratic distribution fits estimate the attainable loss and effective hyperparameter dimension. Joint scaling laws are fit on 4M-34M models, research decisions use 67M-134M validation scales, and 268M is reserved as test. A separate Pre-Norm/Post-Norm study applies four diagnostics: tuned-tail emergence, sensitivity reduction with scale, loss-capability correspondence, and scaling-law validation.
assumptions: The composition of pretraining data remains fixed, so equal pretraining loss is a usable proxy for equal downstream capability across the compared model families.
The lower tail of random-search scores is well approximated by a low-rank quadratic plus additive normal noise over a sufficiently large near-optimal region.
Uniform sampling on the chosen linear, log, and logit hyperparameter coordinates gives a meaningful Monte Carlo measure of near-optimal volume.
Effective parameter count, defined from per-token FLOPs, makes compute approximately 6pd and supports comparisons across sampled architectures.
The architecture and optimization regime do not undergo an unobserved phase change between the 4M-34M fitting range and the 67M-268M held-out range.
Comparing architectures beyond observed scales requires an additional judgment about whether their irreducible-loss asymptotes should be shared.

techniques.role: Samples hundreds of optimizer and architecture configurations per small scale so scaling laws are fit to near-optimal runs rather than typical under-tuned runs.
Fits the lower tail of validation losses to test whether search reached the local optimum and to estimate attainable loss, noise, concentration, and intrinsic hyperparameter dimension.
Counts attention and unembedding compute while excluding embedding lookup so parameter-token products remain proportional to training FLOPs.
Branches decay phases from eight checkpoints of one stable-phase run, producing multiple token-budget observations without retraining each schedule from scratch.
Separates fitting, research validation, and final test model sizes to measure genuine small-to-larger-scale extrapolation.
Verifies on inexpensive downstream tasks that compared fixed-data architectures follow a shared capability-versus-pretraining-loss relation.
Combines tail fit, tuning sensitivity, capability correspondence, and near-data scaling instead of reducing an architecture decision to one far-extrapolated loss.

evaluations.setting: Scaling-law fit on 4M-34M effective-parameter Llama-style models and evaluation on 67M-268M held-out scales
evaluations.metric: Held-out mean-squared error in validation bits per character
evaluations.result: Budget-specific tuning reduces test MSE by 50%, and adding learning-rate decay reduces it by a further reported 98% relative to the preceding recipe.
evaluations.baseline: Best final run at each model scale without budget-specific tuning or decay

evaluations.setting: Randomly subsampled hyperparameter searches at the small fitting scales
evaluations.metric: Visibility and held-out precision of the fitted joint parameter-data scaling law
evaluations.result: 4 and 16 configurations do not reveal a reliable law; 64 reveals one with weak extrapolation; 256 produces the accurate reported fit.
evaluations.baseline: Increasing search budgets drawn from the full sweep

evaluations.setting: Full model-ladder random search from about 4M through 268M effective parameters
evaluations.metric: Random-search score distribution and noisy-quadratic effective dimension gamma
evaluations.result: Near-optimal probability mass increases with scale and gamma trends down toward one, with parameter growth contributing more than additional tokens.
evaluations.baseline: Smaller models and shorter token budgets under the same search-coordinate distribution

evaluations.setting: Full hyperparameter-surface prediction trained on small scales and tested at 67M, 134M, and 268M
evaluations.result: The best reported dynamic-optima surface model obtains 0.002824, 0.004401, and 0.006630 MSE; the tuned-frontier scaling law obtains 0.000011, 0.000025, and 0.000020.
evaluations.baseline: Static quadratic, polynomial, dynamic-curvature, fully dynamic, MLP, and parameter-token-only surface models

evaluations.setting: Pre-Norm versus Post-Norm at 4M and 34M fitting scales with 134M validation
evaluations.metric: Noisy-quadratic fit, sensitivity distribution, loss-capability relation, and held-out scaling error
evaluations.result: Both architectures exhibit the expected tail and common loss-capability trends, but Post-Norm retains a suboptimal loss mode and poorer extrapolation; Pre-Norm scales better throughout the observed compute range.
evaluations.baseline: Matched model/data distributions with normalization placement changed

limitations: Author-stated: far extrapolation amplifies sampling error in the irreducible-loss estimate even when a scaling law is locally accurate.
Author-stated: the methodology is model-centric; changing the pretraining data breaks the loss-capability correspondence on which its cheap downstream proxy relies.
Author-stated: the decline in effective hyperparameter dimension may depend on parameterization, including maximal-update parameterizations, and its limits are not established.
Author-stated: simple interpretable models do not accurately capture how the complete hyperparameter surface changes with scale.
Reviewer-identified: the largest held-out model is 268M effective parameters, so the study validates one order of magnitude of transfer rather than contemporary billion-to-frontier scaling.

Reviewer-identified: the experiments use one Llama-style recipe, one fixed corpus composition, and mostly fixed random seeds; architecture, data, tokenizer, and stochastic-training generality remain unmeasured.

Reviewer-identified: an exhaustive small-model sweep still contains thousands of runs, and the paper gives relative compute arguments but no complete GPU-hour or energy accounting for the proposed workflow.

Reviewer-identified: the Pre-Norm/Post-Norm conclusion beyond the measured range is sensitive to whether the two laws are forced to share an irreducible error, an assumption the experiment cannot test.

Reviewer-identified: downstream correspondence is checked only on small-scale multiple-choice tasks that show signal; it does not establish equivalence on generative, safety, calibration, or late-emerging capabilities.
failure_modes: A small random grid misses the narrow tuned tail and produces noise that looks like a broken scaling law.
Fitting the best final configuration once per scale conflates token-budget effects with hyperparameter mismatch at intermediate checkpoints.
Far extrapolation ranks models by unstable estimates of the asymptotic loss rather than evidence near the measured compute range.
A data or tokenizer change shifts the capability-versus-loss curve, invalidating loss-only architecture selection.
The near-optimal surface changes coordinates under a new parameterization, so a dimension estimate or transferred rule may not survive the implementation change.
A new architecture has a multimodal or discontinuous tuning surface that does not exhibit the noisy-quadratic tail on the available search budget.
Fixed-seed comparisons mistake a favorable or unfavorable stochastic trajectory for a hyperparameter-surface property.
A shared-asymptote constraint forces a preferred long-range ordering that disappears when each architecture has its own irreducible loss.
reusable_insights: Treat failure of an expected scaling regularity as a diagnostic for tuning, implementation, or regime mismatch before treating it as a scientific result.
Spend search budget where the hyperparameter surface is narrow: small models are cheap per run but can require far more configurations than larger ones.
Reserve genuinely larger scales for validation and final test instead of using every scale to choose the fitting recipe.
Compare candidate ideas near the observed compute range and report sensitivity to asymptotic assumptions rather than announcing a winner from one long extrapolation.
When data is fixed, use pretraining loss as a cost coordinate and separately verify that the capability-loss relation survives the architectural intervention.
Model the tuned frontier if the goal is architecture selection; predicting every suboptimal configuration can be much harder and unnecessary.
Carry hyperparameters upward with simple scale rules only after measuring that the near-optimal volume broadens with scale.
open_questions: Does the fall in effective hyperparameter dimension persist for muP-style parameterizations, MoE models, post-training, and billion-parameter scales?
Can adaptive search reach the noisy-quadratic tail with tens rather than hundreds of configurations while retaining a valid stopping diagnostic?
How many random-seed replicates are required to separate surface geometry from stochastic optimization noise at each scale?
Can data-centric interventions be evaluated cheaply using distribution-aware loss coordinates or capability probes that remain comparable after corpus changes?
Which conditions justify sharing irreducible-loss terms across architectures, and can those conditions be falsified before far extrapolation?
Do small-model rankings transfer for capabilities that are absent or unmeasurable at 4M-268M parameters?
Can prospective predictions to multi-billion-parameter held-out runs validate the workflow without using those runs to revise it?

competitive_landscape.title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Porian et al. already show that warmup duration, last-layer compute accounting, and scale-dependent optimizer tuning reconcile Kaplan- and Chinchilla-style laws. This paper broadens the intervention to hundreds of random configurations down to 4M parameters, models the near-optimal loss distribution, and proposes declining intrinsic hyperparameter dimension as the reason tuning becomes easier.

competitive_landscape.title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
competitive_landscape.difference: Wortsman et al. deliberately reproduce large-scale instability in small models by raising learning rates and evaluate warmup, weight decay, muP, activation norms, and gradient norms. The present work targets tuned-frontier loss and architecture selection rather than instability alone, but inherits the broader premise that small-scale sweeps need scale-aware optimizer controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Predictable Scale: Part I -- Optimal Hyperparameter Scaling Law in Large Language Model Pretraining
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. fit explicit optimal learning-rate and batch-size laws from 3,700 models across dense/MoE shapes and data distributions, reporting near-optimal held-out settings. This paper instead searches a wider joint space at much smaller scales, measures the volume and intrinsic dimension of its near-optimal region, and recommends diagnostics rather than one universal plug-in law.

competitive_landscape.title: Configuration-to-Performance Scaling Law with Neural Ansatz
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. learn a neural mapping from full heterogeneous training configurations to performance using public logs and report 20-40% lower error than a configuration-agnostic Chinchilla law. This study uses controlled new experiments, finds full-surface extrapolation substantially worse than tuned-frontier prediction, and is aimed at evaluating novel architectural changes rather than familiar logged configurations.

competitive_landscape.title: Language models scale reliably with over-training and on downstream tasks
competitive_landscape.difference: Gadre et al. fit over-training and downstream power laws using 104 models from 11M to 6.9B parameters and validate predictions hundreds of times beyond fit compute. The present paper pushes the lower endpoint to 4M, emphasizes exhaustive tuning and held-out architecture decisions, and replaces direct downstream extrapolation with a fixed-data loss-capability correspondence plus explicit warnings about irregular tasks.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: predictable parameter-data scaling exists at models as small as roughly 4M effective parameters, becomes visible only on an extensively tuned frontier, and is easier to exploit at larger scale because the near-optimal hyperparameter surface loses intrinsic dimensions; combining that observation with noisy-quadratic and capability-loss diagnostics yields a practical small-scale research methodology. Primary prior work already established scale-dependent tuning as a source of scaling-law disagreement, used small models as instability proxies, fit explicit hyperparameter scaling laws, and predicted performance from full configurations. Reviewer inference: the strongest incremental novelty is the unusually dense controlled random search showing near-optimal volume expansion and a fitted gamma trending toward one, together with a disciplined architecture-case-study protocol. The Pre-Norm result itself is a recovery of known behavior, and the evidence does not yet establish transfer to frontier scale or to data-centric research.
reviewer_notes: The full main text, experimental appendix, search distributions, fitting protocol, implementation details, and full-surface comparison were checked through page 29. Percent improvements are reported as stated because absolute Figure 4 values are not printed in extracted text. Author claims about small-scale predictability are separated from reviewer judgments about the 268M ceiling, fixed seeds, total search cost, and shared-asymptote choice. Competitive mechanisms and identifiers were checked on primary arXiv/OpenReview records.
